title: Restore the disposer returned by the extension and hook `on()` APIs
wave: Wave 1 — Lifecycle foundation (work items W1, W2, W3, W5)
one_line: Make `pi.on(event, handler)` hand back a one-shot unsubscribe function that removes only that exact handler and deletes the event's Map key when the list empties — on both the extension API and the hook API.
user_visible_effect: None directly — no UI, no output, no default behaviour changes. The returned disposer is simply an unused return value until a later work item (W8 cache warmer) registers and calls one. The user-visible effect is negative: an extension author who already wrote `const off = pi.on(...)` gets a working `off()` instead of `undefined`, and no existing caller is affected because TypeScript previously returned `void` so nothing could have been assigned.

test_contract.summary: Withdrawing one handler registration removes exactly that handler, leaves its siblings registered and still firing, and leaves no empty event key behind. A repeated dispose is inert rather than evicting a neighbour that shifted into the freed slot.
test_contract.what_a_consumer_observes_if_it_regresses: If removal were a blind `splice(indexOf(originalFn))` with no identity guarantee, or a blind `splice(0, 1)`, then disposing handler A would silently unregister handler B. Because every dispatch site guards on `handlers && handlers.length > 0` (extensions/runner.ts:1163, hooks/runner.ts:173) and `handlers.length === 0` (hooks/runner.ts:286), the failure is NOT a crash — it is a handler that simply stops running, with no error anywhere. That is the contract worth defending. If the Map key is not deleted on the last removal, the key set grows by one event name per disposed registration across extension reloads; a slow memory leak, likewise silent. If the hooks disposer is never wired (see plan_corrections #5), `off()` is `undefined` and the caller throws `TypeError: off is not a function`.

cases.name: sibling survives a single removal
cases.asserts: Register three handlers on one event, dispose the FIRST, assert the stored list is exactly [B, C] (length 2, and the surviving array contains the original function identities in order). This is identity-safe removal, not a blind shift.
cases.defends: A disposer that splices the wrong element silently disables a handler that the caller never unregistered. The assertion is on function identity, not on a count, because a count-only assertion also passes for a swap-the-wrong-two bug.

cases.name: Map key is deleted when the list empties
cases.asserts: Dispose the last remaining handler and assert `handlers.has(event) === false` — asserted DIRECTLY on the Map, not via dispatch.
cases.defends: The only-splice-naive port leaves an empty array under the key. Critically: nothing in the codebase iterates the handlers Map's keys (verified — every reader is a `.get(eventType)` plus a length guard), so an empty leftover array is behaviourally invisible and a dispatch-based assertion would pass on the broken implementation. This case must read the Map.

cases.name: double dispose is inert
cases.asserts: Register A, B, C. Dispose B (the MIDDLE one) -> list is [A, C]. Dispose B again -> list is STILL [A, C] and length is 2.
cases.defends: This is the neighbour-shift trap the whole item exists to prevent. After the first splice, C has moved into the slot B occupied. A disposer keyed on a captured INDEX rather than identity evicts C on the second call — a handler the caller never touched disappears, and the handler list silently shrinks on every retry. `indexOf` identity + `=== -1` early return is what makes the second call a no-op.

cases.name: a caller that ignores the return value is unaffected
cases.asserts: In a temp hook module / inline extension factory, call `api.on(event, h)` as a bare statement (discarding the return) and then register a second handler for the same event; assert the list has both handlers in order and `handlers.has(event)` is true.
cases.defends: The return type changed from `void` to `() => void` on a public extension/hook API. Existing extension and hook modules in the wild discard that value; if the refactor had accidentally changed the registration path (double-push, early return, reordering) these callers would break with no compile error, because a discarded return value type-checks either way.

banned: mock.module() — mutates the global module registry and leaks across files (Bun #12823). Use the exported loader entry points instead; neither needs it.

Bare not.toThrow() or non-empty checks — they cannot distinguish the fixed implementation from the broken one.
Long-lived globalThis mutations: every globalThis key stashed by a test must be deleted in afterEach.

blocks: W2 — the reverse-order, error-isolating drain helper is the template for the teardown queue in W12, and teardown can only drain disposers that exist.

W8 — the cache warmer registers a disposer on session teardown; against today's `void` return it has nothing to call and an in-flight request leaks. This is the plan's stated 'must land before W8' dependency and the reason W1 is first in Wave 1.
effort: S — roughly 35-45 changed lines across 5 production files (2 return-type-only type files, 2 impl sites, 1 new 8-line helper) plus one ~120-line test file. Larger than the plan's earlier ~15 because there is a second type file and a second implementation.
risk: The `as HookAPI` cast at hooks/loader.ts:128 is lenient enough that changing hooks/types.ts WITHOUT the hooks/loader.ts impl may still type-check cleanly — TypeScript's return-type-void rule makes `(…) => () => void` assignable to a signature returning `void`, so the cast does not complain in either direction. The extension half is safe (ConcreteExtensionAPI `implements ExtensionAPI` at line 179 is a hard check), but the hooks half can ship broken code that compiles. `bun check` is therefore NOT sufficient evidence for the hooks disposer; only the runtime test case that actually calls the returned closure proves it. The second-order risk is writing the disposer to remove a *wrapper* rather than the pushed value: the plan claims extensions wrap handlers, which is FALSE here (both impls push `handler` verbatim — extensions/loader.ts:212, hooks/loader.ts:97), so copying a wrapped-handler port from the reference would be a `indexOf === -1` silent no-op.
open_questions: Should the helper live in `extensibility/utils.ts` (recommended — both loaders already import from it) or be inlined twice? The AGENTS.md dedup rule argues for the shared helper; a reviewer preferring the minimal 4-file diff may argue for inlining. This is the one genuine design choice in the item.

Does `HandlerFn` need to be exported from `extensibility/utils.ts`, or should the helper type the Map as `Map<string, (...args: unknown[]) => Promise<unknown>>` inline? `HandlerFn` is currently a private alias duplicated in extensions/loader.ts:61, extensions/types.ts:1696, and hooks/loader.ts:21. Consolidating it is tempting but is a wider refactor than W1 should absorb.

plan_corrections.claim: The likeliest mistake is splicing the ORIGINAL handler rather than the wrapper that was actually pushed — 'extensions wrap handlers, so indexOf(originalFn) is -1'.
plan_corrections.correction: Neither implementation wraps. `extensions/loader.ts:212` is a literal `list.push(handler)` and `hooks/loader.ts:97` is `handlers.get(event)!.push(handler)` — the caller's function object is stored by reference, unwrapped. The class constructor (extensions/loader.ts:196-207) rebinds prototype methods onto the instance for detached-callback safety but never touches handler identity, and there is no Proxy on the API object in the registration path. So a disposer that closes over `handler` and does `indexOf(handler)` is CORRECT. Porting a wrapped-handler disposer from the (nonexistent) reference would produce a permanent silent no-op — which is the opposite failure from the one the plan warns about, and the plan's warning would send a careful engineer to add a needless lookup indirection.
plan_corrections.evidence: `sed -n '210,214p' packages/coding-agent/src/extensibility/extensions/loader.ts` -> `list.push(handler);`; `sed -n '93,98p' packages/coding-agent/src/extensibility/hooks/loader.ts` -> `handlers.get(event)!.push(handler);`; `grep -n 'Proxy'` in extensions/loader.ts -> no hits (only extensions/wrapper.ts, for tool definitions).

plan_corrections.claim: Because of the `as HookAPI` cast, both implementations must keep signature-compatible types or the cast breaks type-check.
plan_corrections.verdict: PARTLY FALSE — holds for extensions, NOT guaranteed for hooks
plan_corrections.correction: The extension half IS enforced: `class ConcreteExtensionAPI implements ExtensionAPI` (extensions/loader.ts:179) is a hard structural check, so changing the 41 overloads without the class method fails `bun check` loudly. The hooks half is NOT guaranteed: a function returning `() => void` is assignable to a signature returning `void` (TypeScript's return-type-void rule), and comparability for an `as` assertion is satisfied if EITHER direction holds — so a hooks/types.ts-only change would most likely still compile and ship a disposer that returns `undefined` at runtime. Consequence for this spec: prove the hooks disposer with the runtime test, not with the type checker. Do not let 'bun check is green' be the evidence for that half.
plan_corrections.evidence: `sed -n '179p'` -> `class ConcreteExtensionAPI implements ExtensionAPI, IExtensionRuntime;`; `sed -n '128p'` -> `} as HookAPI;` (an assertion, not an `implements`). Reasoning is a type-system argument, not a reproduced error — treat as strong-but-unexecuted; the runtime test is the real guard.
